Unit 4 check

About 20 minutes: one fresh question for each part of every outcome of Unit 4, plus two from earlier units to keep them sharp. It is not graded and only you see it.

An outcome becomes Secure when you have answered a question on each of its parts right first time, without a hint or the solution, here in this check. When all 5 are secure you are ready to try Canvas Quiz 4 (due Sun 8 Nov). Already know this material? Take the check before the lessons and skip what is secure.

Review: Unit 4 · Lesson 4.2 · Exponentials and logs

ChooseRules of exponentials and logarithms4b

Which of these is equal to ln⁡(32)\ln\left(3^{2}\right)ln(32)?

2ln⁡32\ln 32ln3
A power inside a logarithm comes out in front: ln⁡(ak)=kln⁡a\ln(a^k) = k\ln aln(ak)=klna.
ln⁡6\ln 6ln6
32=93^{2} = 932=9, not 2×32 \times 32×3.
3ln⁡23\ln 23ln2
The base and the power have swapped places: the power comes out in front.
ln⁡3+2\ln 3 + 2ln3+2
A power inside becomes a multiplier outside, not something added.
ChooseRead a log scale4b

The graph shows three models for the value of an investment over 20 years, drawn with plt.yscale("log"). Which curve shows exponential growth (the same percentage increase every year)?

Curve B
On a log scale, equal steps up the axis are equal factors. Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor in every equal time step, so it is a straight line: curve B.
Curve A
Curve A grows by the same amount each year (linear growth). On a log scale that bends over, because each extra amount is a smaller and smaller factor.
Curve C
Curve C is not a straight line on the log scale, so its growth factor changes over time: it is not exponential.
None of them: exponential growth would curve upwards
On an ordinary axis it would; on a log scale, exponential growth is a straight line.

Review: Unit 4 · Lesson 4.4 · Walking downhill

ChooseGradient descent in code4e

What does this program print?

c = 2.0
eta = 1.25
for step in range(3):
    slope = 2 * (c + 2)
    c = c - eta * slope
print(round(c, 4))
-15.5
Each step multiplies the distance to −2-2−2 by 1−1.25×2=−1.51 - 1.25 \times 2 = -1.51−1.25×2=−1.5: after 3 steps c=−15.5c = -15.5c=−15.5. The steps overshoot and grow: this learning rate is too large.
169.5
That is what c = c + eta * slope would give: stepping uphill. The update subtracts.
18.25
That is after 4 steps. range(3) runs the loop 3 times.
7.0
That is after 2 steps. range(3) runs the loop 3 times.

Your answerRead a log scale4b

The graph shows the number of users of an app over 15 years, drawn with plt.yscale("log"). How many years does it take to grow a hundredfold (×100)?

That is the number of factors of 10 the line climbs. The question asks how long one hundredfold growth takes.
That is the time to grow tenfold, one gridline. A hundredfold is two gridlines: 10×1010 \times 1010×10.
That is the time for the whole line, which climbs 3 gridlines: 3 factors of 10.
On a log scale each gridline is ten times the one below.
The line climbs 3 gridlines in 15 years, at a steady rate.
Solution

The line climbs from 100 to 100 000: 3 factors of 10 in 15 years, so one factor of 10 every 5 years, and a factor of 100 every 10 years.

Rules of exponentials and logarithms

Choose4b

Which of these is equal to ln⁡(53)\ln\left(5^{3}\right)ln(53)?

3ln⁡53\ln 53ln5
A power inside a logarithm comes out in front: ln⁡(ak)=kln⁡a\ln(a^k) = k\ln aln(ak)=klna.
(ln⁡5)3\left(\ln 5\right)^{3}(ln5)3
The power comes out in front as a multiplier: ln⁡(ak)=kln⁡a\ln(a^k) = k \ln aln(ak)=klna, not (ln⁡a)k(\ln a)^k(lna)k.
5ln⁡35\ln 35ln3
The base and the power have swapped places: the power comes out in front.
ln⁡5+3\ln 5 + 3ln5+3
A power inside becomes a multiplier outside, not something added.

ln⁡14\ln 14ln14
Adding logarithms multiplies the numbers inside: ln⁡a+ln⁡b=ln⁡(ab)=ln⁡14\ln a + \ln b = \ln(ab) = \ln 14lna+lnb=ln(ab)=ln14.

ln⁡2×ln⁡7\ln 2 \times \ln 7ln2×ln7
The log of a product is a sum of logs; the product of two logs is something else.

Read a log scale

Taught in Lesson 4.2 · Rules for derivatives — powers, exponentials, logs.

Your answer4b

The graph shows the number of bacteria in a culture over 12 years, drawn with plt.yscale("log"). How many years does it take to grow tenfold (×10)?

That is the number of factors of 10 the line climbs. The question asks how long one tenfold growth takes.
That is the time for the whole line, which climbs 3 gridlines: 3 factors of 10.
On a log scale each gridline is ten times the one below.
The line climbs 3 gridlines in 12 years, at a steady rate.
Solution

The line climbs from 100 to 100 000: 3 factors of 10 in 12 years, so one factor of 10 every 4 years.

Review: Unit 4 · Lesson 4.2 · Reading a log scale

Choose4b

The graph shows three models for the number of users of an app over 10 years, drawn with plt.yscale("log"). Which curve shows exponential growth (the same percentage increase every year)?

Curve B
On a log scale, equal steps up the axis are equal factors. Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor in every equal time step, so it is a straight line: curve B.
Curve A
Curve A grows by the same amount each year (linear growth). On a log scale that bends over, because each extra amount is a smaller and smaller factor.
Curve C
Curve C is not a straight line on the log scale, so its growth factor changes over time: it is not exponential.
None of them: exponential growth would curve upwards
On an ordinary axis it would; on a log scale, exponential growth is a straight line.

Classify a stationary point

Taught in Lesson 4.3 · Peaks, valleys and gradients.

Choose4c

f(x)=x3+6x2+9x−1f(x) = x^{3} + 6x^{2} + 9x - 1f(x)=x3+6x2+9x−1 has a stationary point at x=−1x = -1x=−1. What kind of point is it?

A local minimum
f′′(x)=6x+12f''(x) = 6x + 12f′′(x)=6x+12, so f′′(−1)=6>0f''(-1) = 6 > 0f′′(−1)=6>0: a local minimum.
A local maximum
f′′(−1)=6f''(-1) = 6f′′(−1)=6, which is not negative.
Neither: fff keeps rising (or keeps falling) through it
f′′(−1)=6≠0f''(-1) = 6 \ne 0f′′(−1)=6=0, so the graph bends one way: f′f'f′ changes sign at x=−1x = -1x=−1.
A point where the graph crosses the xxx-axis
f′(−1)=0f'(-1) = 0f′(−1)=0 says the slope is zero, not the value: f(−1)=−5f(-1) = -5f(−1)=−5.
Choose4c

A smooth function has f′(1)=0f'(1) = 0f′(1)=0 and f′′(1)=1f''(1) = 1f′′(1)=1. What does fff have at x=1x = 1x=1?

A local minimum
f′′(1)=1>0f''(1) = 1 > 0f′′(1)=1>0: the slope is increasing, from negative to positive, so the graph bends up like a valley floor.
A local maximum

Choose4e

This loop runs gradient descent on f(c)=(c−7)2f(c) = (c - 7)^2f(c)=(c−7)2, whose minimum is at c=7c = 7c=7. The learning rate is left blank. For which value of eta does ccc move further and further away from the minimum?

c = 10.0
eta = ___
for step in range(100):
    slope = 2 * (c - 7)
    c = c - eta * slope
print(c)
eta = 1.2
Each step multiplies the distance to 777 by 1−2η=−1.41 - 2\eta = -1.41−2η=−1.4. That is bigger than 1 in size, so every step overshoots further than the last and ccc runs away.
eta = 0.01
This rate is small: each step multiplies the distance to 777 by 0.980.980.98, so ccc creeps towards the minimum slowly, but it gets there.
eta = 0.25
Each step multiplies the distance to 777 by 0.50.50.5, so ccc settles quickly at the minimum.
eta = 0.9
Each step multiplies the distance by −0.8-0.8−0.8: ccc overshoots and zig-zags, but the zig-zags shrink, so it still converges.

This loop should find the minimum of f(c)=(c−4)2f(c) = (c - 4)^2f(c)=(c−4)2, which is at c=4c = 4c=4, and print it. It does not. Which single change makes it print 4.0? (Lines are numbered from 1.)

c = 2
eta = 0.1
for step in range(100):
    slope = (c - 4) ** 2
    c = c - eta * slope
print(round(c, 3))
Change line 4 to slope = 2 * (c - 4)
The update needs the slope f′(c)=2(c−4)f'(c) = 2(c - 4)f′(c)=2(c−4), not the value f(c)=(c−4)2f(c) = (c - 4)^2f(c)=(c−4)2.
Change line 2 to eta = 0.01
A smaller step does not help: the loop follows (c−4)2(c - 4)^2(c−4)2 instead of its slope, which is never negative, so ccc only ever moves left.
Change line 5 to c = c + eta * slope
Now ccc creeps towards 4, but the steps η(c−4)2\eta(c - 4)^2η(c−4)2 shrink so fast that after 100 steps it is still short. The update needs the slope 2(c−4)2(c - 4)2(c−4).
Change line 3 to for step in range(1000):
More steps do not help: the loop follows (c−4)2(c - 4)^2(c−4)2, not its slope, and ccc keeps moving left.
Choose4e

This loop should find the minimum of f(c)=(c−3)2f(c) = (c - 3)^2f(c)=(c−3)2, which is at c=3c = 3c=3, and print it. It does not. Which single change makes it print 3.0? (Lines are numbered from 1.)

c = 9
eta = 0.1
for step in range(100):
    slope = 2 * (c - 3)
    c - eta * slope
print(round(c, 3))
Change line 5 to c = c - eta * slope
c - eta * slope works out the new value but throws it away: c never changes. Assign it back to c.
Change line 2 to eta = 0.01
The learning rate is fine; the new value is never stored in c.
Change line 3 to for step in range(1000):
More passes change nothing: c is never updated.
Change line 5 to c = eta * slope
That replaces c by the step itself, not by the old value minus the step.
